body: Feeling like a fraud at work is common, and it tends to ease with practice. For the next ninety days, expect one short note a day to help you settle into the place you have earned.
No need to change anything today. Just notice the moment at work when you felt most like you might be found out.
Imposter feelings often arrive with something new: a promotion, a big meeting, a fresh team. Notice what was new when yours last showed up.
Listen for the phrase "they will realise" in your head. Who are "they", and what exactly do you fear they will realise?
Many capable people feel this way, including those you quietly admire. The feeling is not a reliable measure of your ability.
Notice how you explain your successes. Luck, timing, help from others? See whether you ever give yourself any of the credit.
Notice what you do to avoid being found out. Over-preparing, staying quiet, working late? Just name the habit for now.
Pay attention to your body before you speak in a meeting. A racing heart is not proof you are out of your depth.
Someone chose to hire you. They looked at your experience and decided you fitted. Their judgement counts for something.
Notice who you compare yourself with at work. Often it is the most confident person in the room, not the most typical.
Feeling unsure and being unqualified are different things. Today, just notice which one is actually happening.
When praise comes your way, what do you do with it? Brush it off, change the subject, explain it away? Observe without judging.
Notice the times you do feel at ease at work, even briefly. What were you doing, and who were you with?
Nobody at your workplace knows everything. Watch for small signs today that others are also figuring things out as they go.
After a fortnight of watching closely, you have a clearer map of when the fraud feeling turns up and when it stays away.
Write down one thing you did well at work this week. Keep it short and factual, as if writing about a colleague.
Start a simple file of evidence: thank-you notes, good feedback, problems you solved. Add one item today.
When someone thanks you today, try saying only "Thank you, I am glad it helped." No disclaimers needed.
Ask one question in a meeting or message that you would normally keep to yourself. Questions are part of doing the job well.
Set a limit on preparation for one task this week. Stop at good enough and see what actually happens.
Say "I do not know yet, but I will find out" once this week. Notice how others respond. It is usually fine.
Look at the skills listed in your job description and tick the ones you already use. Count them honestly.
Share one small idea with a colleague before it feels finished. Early ideas are how good work begins.
Ask a trusted colleague what they think you are good at. Listen to the answer without arguing with it.
Notice one mistake someone senior makes this week. It does not make them a fraud, and yours do not make you one either.
Write the fearful thought "I do not belong here" on paper. Underneath, write three facts about how you got here.
Take up a little more space in one meeting: sit where you can be seen, or speak in the first ten minutes.
If a task feels beyond you, break it into three steps and do the first one. Ability often shows up once you begin.
Hold back one apology today that is not needed. "Sorry to bother you" can often become "Have you got a minute?"
Tell one person you trust about a work fear, out loud. Fears spoken aloud usually shrink a little.
Look back at a past job or course where you once felt out of place. How did you feel by the end of it?
Offer help to a newer colleague with something you know well. Teaching shows you how much you have learned.
Read your evidence file before a hard meeting or task. Let it remind you that you have a track record.
Notice the inner voice that says "anyone could have done that". Reply: "Perhaps, but I am the one who did."
Ask for feedback on one piece of work, specifically. Precise feedback is far easier to use than vague worry.
Accept one compliment today without shrinking it. Let it land, even if it feels awkward.
Pick one area where you want to grow and treat it as learning, rather than as a test you might fail.
Write a short note on what you would say to a friend who felt like a fraud in your job. Then read it to yourself.
Volunteer for one modest task you would usually leave to others. Choose something stretching but manageable.
When you finish something today, pause for ten seconds and register it as done. Completed work counts.
Imagine you have finally been "found out". What would people actually discover? Most likely, someone who cares and tries.
Think about how you last described your role to someone outside work. Did you play it down? Try saying it plainly next time.
Notice one thing you now do easily that once felt hard at work. That gap is real growth, not luck.
Ask yourself what a fair manager would say about your last month. Write it down in their words, not your critic's.
Put your hand up for something visible, such as presenting a small update. A short, plain slot is plenty.
Spend five minutes adding to your evidence file. Look at how much it has grown since you started.
Notice which experiments felt surprisingly easy. Those are good candidates to become everyday habits.
Talk about your work in the first person once this week. "I fixed the report" rather than "the report got fixed".
Before a new task, remind yourself that learning on the job is part of every role, including the most senior ones.
Let one piece of work go out without a final, anxious re-check. Trust the checks you have already done.
Voice a little less self-doubt aloud today and watch how colleagues respond. Often nothing changes, except how you feel.
Recall a call you made at work that others went along with and that worked. Good outcomes rarely happen by accident.
If you have a mentor or a supportive manager, tell them a little about these feelings. Good leaders have usually had them too.
Treat a moment of not knowing as information, not exposure. It simply tells you what to learn next.
Look at your calendar and notice the meetings you were invited to. People include you because your view is useful.
Try saying "I think" rather than "This might be silly, but". Give your ideas a fair start.
Celebrate one small win with someone today, even with a quick message. Shared good news feels more real.
Notice when a thought about being found out passes without you acting on it. That is a skill growing.
Write down the qualities you bring that are not on any job description: steadiness, kindness, care for detail.
Ask yourself which experiment you would miss if you stopped. That answer is worth paying attention to.
Look back over the last few weeks. Which two or three experiments helped you feel most settled at work? Keep those close.
From here, the aim shifts from trying new approaches to practising the few that already help you feel at home at work.
Imposter feelings may flare again with a new role or a big project. A flare does not cancel the progress you have made.
If a day goes badly at work, separate the event from the verdict. One weak meeting is not proof that you never belonged.
Notice whether you are waiting to feel confident before you act. Often confidence follows action rather than leading it.
Some workplaces really do make people feel they do not fit. If that is part of your story, the problem is not only in your head.
Return to your evidence file on a day when the old doubts are loud. Read it slowly, one entry at a time.
Be kind to the version of you who first started this job. They were brave to walk in on that first day.
Think about what you would be free to do if you stopped worrying about being found out. Take one small step in that direction.
When criticism comes, take what is useful and leave the rest. Feedback about one task is not a ruling on your place.
Notice if you are working twice as hard to prove yourself. Ask whether that extra effort is still needed.
Share your view first in one discussion this week, before you hear what others think.
If an old fear returns, greet it by name: "Ah, the fraud feeling again." Naming it gives you a little distance.
Look at how patiently you treat colleagues who are still learning. Offer yourself that same patience.
Recall a recent moment when you knew the answer and someone relied on you. Let that memory sit for a while.
Belonging is not something you wait to be given. It also grows each time you show up and take part.
A setback this week? Note what you will try differently, then put it down. Dwelling rarely teaches more.
Notice one way your work has helped someone else this month. Your contribution reaches further than you think.
Consider what being experienced really means. It is not knowing everything; it is knowing how to find out.
Tell a colleague about something you are proud of. Plain, factual pride is not boasting.
On a doubtful day, do one routine task you know well. Competence in small things steadies the bigger picture.
Ask yourself whether your standards for yourself match the ones you hold for others. If not, which would be fairer?
Write a short line about the kind of colleague you want to be. Let that guide you more than the fear of exposure.
If a new challenge appears, remind yourself that feeling stretched is what growth feels like from the inside.
Notice how much less time you now spend rehearsing worst cases. That freed attention is yours to use.
Look again at your list of qualities from earlier. Choose one to lean on deliberately this week.
Write down the three habits from these weeks that helped you feel you belong. Keep them somewhere easy to find.
Make a short plan for the next time the old feeling returns: what to read, who to talk to, which step to take.
You may never feel entirely certain at work, and that is normal. You can belong and still have questions.
Look at how you describe your job now compared with three months ago. Notice any change in the words you choose.
Keep adding to your evidence file now and then. It becomes more useful the longer it grows.
Your seat at work was never a mistake. Keep turning up as yourself, and trust the person who earned it.
